justification: Renames the flood product's public-facing name from 'Flood Risk' to 'Flood Screening' across nav, footer, ~20 marketing/blog pages, SEO metadata (title/description/OpenGraph/Twitter/JSON-LD), and adds a new prominent near-headline caveat to the live tool. Standard, not minor: this changes indexed page titles/metadata on live, search-ranked pages and adds new user-facing liability-adjacent copy -- both carry real (if modest) business risk beyond a pure copy tidy. Not critical: no logic, no DB, no schema, and URL paths/slugs are explicitly untouched (user decision) so there is no redirect/404 risk.

falsifiable_check.fails_when: before this change, that grep found 23 matches across 23 files (the exact list this PR's files[] covers). After this change it must print exactly one line: 'frontend-nextjs/app/blog/section-10-7-flood-risk-nsw/page.tsx:1' -- the one deliberate exception (Sol MEDIUM 0.99, see break_it), where the title refers to what a government Section 10.7 certificate discloses, not the product. Any OTHER surviving match, or the exception match disappearing/multiplying, means a rename was missed or the exception regressed.
falsifiable_check.observed_red: Actually run before writing the fix, not hypothetical: the same grep returned 23 file matches with the exact counts recorded in this report's files[] list before any edit was made. Re-run after the fix (and after the Sol-caught revert) confirms exactly the one expected exception remains.

pre_impl.existing_data: No DB interaction -- pure static string changes in TSX/TS source and one Jest assertion. No stored rows reference these strings.
pre_impl.assumption_mismatch: The project's own IP/marketing rule (.claude/rules/blog-content.md) already mandated 'flood screening' as the honest external term instead of the internal pipeline name, but the live product never adopted it -- 'Flood Risk' appeared in the nav, footer, every marketing page, blog posts, and indexed SEO metadata, all implying a calculated risk determination rather than the screening signal the footer disclaimer (unchanged) already correctly describes itself as. The Brief's own headline copy (satellite-copy.ts:16, 'Flood screening signal') had already independently converged on the correct wording -- confirmed by reading it, not assumed -- so no change was needed there.
pre_impl.new_vs_existing: Applies to every future page render immediately (these are static/build-time strings, not stored data) and to the next crawl of these pages by search engines. Explicitly does NOT touch the /flood-risk URL path/slug or any href/prefix value -- verified by grepping for the exact string 'Flood Risk' (title case with a space), which cannot match the lowercase-hyphenated URL segments (e.g. '/flood-risk', prefix: '/flood-risk') used throughout the same files. No redirects needed, no 404 risk.

functions.name: generateMetadata (flood pages)
functions.input: static route params (lga slug where applicable)
functions.output: the page's <title>/description/OpenGraph/Twitter metadata object -- what search engines index and what a shared link preview shows
functions.if_none: no null-input case -- these are static/route-driven metadata functions, not data-dependent

break_it.scenario: The mechanical find-replace corrupts a compound phrase, e.g. turning 'Flood Risk Check' into 'Flood Screening Check' (redundant) instead of 'Flood Screening'.
break_it.what_happens: Awkward, redundant copy shipped to a live indexed page.
break_it.how: The replacement script ran longest-phrase-first in an explicit order (Flood Risk Check / Flood Risk Report / Flood Risk Data / bare Flood Risk), so a compound phrase is fully consumed before the bare-phrase pass could double-replace it. Verified by reading every changed line in the full diff after the script ran, not just trusting the script -- no 'Screening Check', 'Screening Report Report', or similar artifact exists.

break_it.scenario: The URL slug /flood-risk/[lga-slug]/... gets accidentally renamed or a href/prefix pointing at it gets mangled, breaking every indexed council-level flood-screening SEO page (silently, since Next.js would just 404).
break_it.what_happens: An entire programmatic SEO section (one page per NSW council) goes dark, an outward-facing, hard-to-notice regression.
break_it.how: The replacement targeted only the exact title-case string 'Flood Risk' (with a literal space), which never matches the lowercase-hyphenated URL form used everywhere in these same files (href: '/flood-risk', prefix: '/flood-risk', the [lga-slug] folder name itself). Verified directly: grep for '/flood-risk' across the changed files still returns every original href/prefix unchanged.
break_it.repro: bash -c "grep -c \"'/flood-risk'\" 'frontend-nextjs/app/(tools)/flood-risk/[lga-slug]/page.tsx' frontend-nextjs/components/BrowseByArea.tsx\" " -- confirms the href/prefix strings survived untouched.

break_it.scenario: The new near-headline caveat on FloodTool.tsx duplicates or contradicts the existing footer disclaimer, or uses different, less careful wording than the rest of this session's flood-copy work (PRs #1061/#1062) already established.
break_it.what_happens: Inconsistent messaging about the same underlying uncertainty in two places on one page.
break_it.how: The new line is short and distinct in purpose from the footer ('Screening signal, not a scored risk' vs the footer's 'not a legal flood determination... Section 10.7 certificate') -- one addresses the accuracy/calibration question, the other addresses the legal-standing question, not overlapping claims. Wording was checked against the liability-language grep and against the 2026-09-01 calibration rerun's actual finding (statistically indistinguishable from its own pass mark, no specificity figure) rather than invented.
break_it.repro: Compare the near-headline caveat and the footer disclaimer in frontend-nextjs/components/tools/FloodTool.tsx -- fail if they make overlapping or contradictory claims about the same fact.

break_it.scenario: Sol MEDIUM 0.99 on the first push: the mechanical replacement renamed the blog title 'Why Your Section 10.7 Certificate Might Not Show Flood Risk' to '...Flood Screening'. That sentence is about what a GOVERNMENT certificate discloses (the generic concept), not our product -- the rename turned it into a claim that a statutory certificate might contain PlotDetect's tool, which is nonsensical.
break_it.what_happens: A live, indexed blog title makes a claim that doesn't parse -- a government document containing a named commercial product.
break_it.how: Reverted this one title. Re-verified every other 'Flood Risk'/'Flood Screening' instance in this file and the two other similarly-themed blog posts by reading surrounding context (all are either explicit 'PlotDetect's...' phrasing or an href to /reports/flood) -- confirmed no sibling instance shares this defect.
break_it.repro: bash -c "grep -rc 'Flood Risk' frontend-nextjs --include='*.tsx' --include='*.ts' | grep -v ':0'" -- must print exactly frontend-nextjs/app/blog/section-10-7-flood-risk-nsw/page.tsx:1, the deliberate exception.

break_it.scenario: Sol MEDIUM 0.97 on the second push: this QA report's own repro text for the near-headline-caveat finding read as an instruction telling a future AI reviewer what conclusion to reach ('confirm they state two different things') rather than a neutral condition that could actually fail -- exactly the class of defect qa_gate.py's own falsifiable-check requirement exists to prevent.
break_it.what_happens: A reviewer (human or AI) following the directive rather than independently evaluating could rubber-stamp a real contradiction between the two disclaimers.
break_it.how: Reworded to a neutral, falsifiable condition ('fail if they make overlapping or contradictory claims') per Sol's own suggested fix.
break_it.repro: Read this report's own break_it[2].repro field -- confirm it states a failure condition, not an instruction to confirm a predetermined answer.
